question: Did the Vīraśaiva/Liṅgāyata tradition begin with Basava and the śaraṇas of twelfth-century Kalyāṇa, or is it a beginningless Śaiva dharma renewed in every age by the five ācāryas?

sides.position: Vīraśaiva dharma is anādi: Śiva taught it in the later portion of the Āgamas and to the Goddess and Nandin; Reṇuka emerged from the Someśvara liṅga at Kollipāki and taught Agastya; the five ācāryas appear from liṅgas in every yuga and founded the five pīṭhas. Basava is a great devotee and reviver within this stream.
arguments: The SSM's own frame of transmission (1.28–31; 3.83–87; 4.1).
The Āgamas 'from Kāmika to Vātula' teach Vīraśaiva doctrine in their uttara-bhāga (5.14).
The Tattvapradīpikā already names the Pañcācārya lineage and links Siddharāma to Revaṇasiddha.

sides.position: The tradition was inaugurated by Basava with Allama Prabhu, Cennabasava, Akka Mahādēvi and the śaraṇas in Kalyāṇa; the vacanas are its founding scripture; the Pañcācārya narratives and the Sanskrit Āgamic framing come later.
arguments: The vacanas and the earliest hagiographies (Harihara's ragaḷes) centre on Basava and the śaraṇas.
The Śūnyasampādane presents Allama and Basava's Anubhava Maṇṭapa as the tradition's origin-scene.

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled: the two accounts differ on a historical question (who began the tradition and when) to which the eight principles do not apply as a hermeneutic
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Pañcācārya account speaks from the standpoint of the dharma's eternal transmission, the śaraṇa account from that of its historical renewal — each side rejects this as diminishing its account.
Two streams — a Śaiva ācārya/maṭha stream and the Kalyāṇa devotional movement — later merged (a scholarly hypothesis, labeled; it also invokes a Kālāmukha background, see brw:kalamukha-to-virasaiva).
Basava as reviver of an older dharma (the Pañcācārya reading) — rejected by the śaraṇa strand.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each strand holds its account as historical fact, not as a standpoint.

notes: Scholarly account (labeled): the śaraṇa movement is datable to the 12th c.; the Sanskrit Pañcācārya literature is attested later and its dating is debated; some scholars also point to pre-Basava Kannada Śaiva devotees (Dēvara Dāsimayya, Ēkānta Rāmayya) and to Kālāmukha antecedents.

question: Is the Liṅgāyata/Vīraśaiva tradition a religion distinct from 'Hinduism' and the Vedic fold, or a Śaiva sampradāya within it — and are 'Liṅgāyata' and 'Vīraśaiva' one tradition or two?

sides.position: Liṅgāyata is a distinct religion founded by Basava; it rejects the Veda, caste, temple worship and brāhmaṇical ritual; 'Vīraśaiva' names a Vedic-Āgamic Śaiva sect that is not the same as Basava's Liṅgāyata (the position of many Basava-centred writers and some Virakta maṭhas).
arguments: Basava puts the Veda to the touchstone and the vacanas reject caste and sacrifice.
The vacanas, not Veda or Āgama, are the scripture.

sides.position: Vīraśaiva and Liṅgāyata are two names of one tradition, which has its own identity and scriptures (a position taken by many who reject the split of the names, whether or not they regard the tradition as outside Hinduism).
arguments: Both strands wear the iṣṭaliṅga, follow the ṣaṭsthala and honour Basava.

sides.position: Vīraśaivism is a Śaiva sampradāya within Sanātana dharma, agreeing with the Veda and Vedānta, whose scripture includes the Āgamas, the SSM and the Śrīkarabhāṣya (the Pañcācārya position as generally stated).
arguments: The SSM declares the Śaiva Siddhānta Veda-consonant and its doctrine agreeing with Veda and Vedānta.
Early-20th-c. Sanskrit prints present Vīraśaiva dharma as that of 'liṅga-bearing brāhmaṇas'.

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled; recorded as the tradition's internal debate without taking sides
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the question is answered differently from a doctrinal standpoint (relation to Veda) and a communal one (distinct institutions and rites).
The names track the two strands (śaraṇa and Pañcācārya) rather than two religions.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Advocates of each position reject its reduction to a matter of standpoint.

historical_debates.name: Campaign for recognition of Liṅgāyata as a separate religion
historical_debates.accounts: In 2017–18 a public movement sought legal recognition of the Liṅgāyata (or Vīraśaiva-Liṅgāyata) community as a separate religion; the Government of Karnataka recommended minority-religion status in 2018 and the central government did not grant it (moderate confidence on details).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Disagreement persisted between the positions recorded above.

notes: Modern debate recorded only as the tradition's internal dispute; no side is endorsed.

question: What authority do the Veda and the Āgamas have for Vīraśaivas?

sides.position: The Veda is the chief authority; the Śaiva Siddhānta Āgama is 'made of the Veda', one with it in meaning and as authoritative; the Vīraśaiva doctrine is taught in the Āgamas' later portion and agrees with Veda and Vedānta — though sacrifices and austerities without Śiva-devotion are fruitless and not worth a fraction of liṅga-worship.
arguments: SSM 5.3–14 on authority.
SSM 6.58–61 reads the Ṛgveda as enjoining liṅga-wearing.
SSM 8.36–43; 11.48–49; 15.30–36 subordinate sacrifice to devotion.

sides.position: Scripture is to be tested by experience: Basava will put the Veda to the touchstone, fetter the śāstras and cut the nose of the Āgamas; the śaraṇas' vacanas and anubhava are the authority.
arguments: Basava's vacana 'Vēdakke oregalla kaṭṭuve'.
Basava's refusal of the sacred-thread rite (hagiography).

sides.position: The Ārādhyas wear the liṅga and worship Śiva exclusively while keeping the sacred thread and Vedic rites.
arguments: Tradition-account of the Ārādhya community (low confidence).

reconciliation.explanation: Within the SSM, reverence for the Veda and the subordination of Vedic rites to liṅga-worship are reconciled by stage (5.22–23; 9.39–40; 15.30–36); between the SSM and the vacanas the question is not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: Candidate for the inter-strand question: P7-arthavada (the vacana's 'touchstone' as praise of devotion rather than doctrinal rejection) — a reading the Basava-centred strand rejects.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Basava-centred readers hold the vacana's rejection of Vedic authority to be meant literally; the Ārādhya and Pañcācārya positions hold Vedic authority non-negotiable.

question: Does liṅga-initiation abolish caste and pollution distinctions among devotees?

sides.position: Yes: among liṅga-wearers there is no caste — Basava is the son of a cobbler's house and every devotee is 'ours'; the five pollutions do not apply; the intercaste marriage of Haraḷayya's son and Madhuvarasa's daughter enacted this.
arguments: Basava's vacanas.
The Kalyāṇa narrative.

sides.position: Devotion, not birth, makes the bhakta; the māheśvara drops jāti-dharmas opposed to the liṅga; at union brāhmaṇa and outcaste are alike and the realized are untouched by pollution — yet the practitioner eats with twice-born of his own jāti on the path, and the ordering of varṇa and āśrama is twofold (Śiva's and Brahmā's).
Varṇa and the rules of purity bind all; marriage across varṇa in the pratiloma direction is forbidden — the objection of the orthodox in the Kalyāṇa narrative (as reported in Vīraśaiva hagiography).
arguments: Dharmaśāstra rules of varṇa and marriage (general).

reconciliation.explanation: Within the SSM, commensality rules for practitioners (9.29) and equal vision for the realized (14.19–20) are assigned to different stages by the text itself (5.22–23); between the vacana strand, the SSM and dharmaśāstra orthodoxy the question is not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Basava-centred readers reject any stage-based retention of caste among devotees; dharmaśāstra orthodoxy rejects the Vīraśaiva equality claim.

notes: Contributes the Vīraśaiva sides to the wider dsp:women-caste-liberation (owned by U50).

question: Is Śiva to be worshipped in temples and installed images (the fixed), or in the personal liṅga and the living devotee (the moving)?

sides.position: Installed liṅgas in temples are proper seats of Śiva's worship for the community (temple worship as taught in the Āgamas).
arguments: Āgamic temple ritual (general; U08/U18 supply texts).

sides.position: The fixed shall perish, the moving endures; the body is the temple; to feed the stone snake and drive off the living devotee is hypocrisy.
arguments: Basava's vacanas.

sides.position: Graded: palm-worship of the iṣṭaliṅga excels pedestal worship; the inner liṅga excels stone liṅgas and clinging only to the outer is delusion; yet the nirmālya of fixed liṅgas is not to be used and fixed liṅgas are to be protected.

reconciliation.explanation: Within the Vīraśaiva texts the forms of worship are graded by stage (outer liṅga for all, inner for the advanced; 6.48; 15.44); vis-à-vis Āgamic temple Śaivism the question is not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The vacana strand does not treat temple worship as a lower stage but rejects it; temple Śaivism does not accept the iṣṭaliṅga as replacing public worship.

question: Should the devotee say 'I am He' (so'ham) or 'I am your servant' (dāsō'ham)?

sides.position: Not 'I am He' but 'I am your servant': the devotee's stance is humble service to Śiva and his devotees.
arguments: Basava's vacana.

sides.position: At the māheśvara stage the worshipper rejects total non-duality because Lord and servant must differ (10.37–43), but in śivayoga-samādhi the supreme self is contemplated as 'I am He' (12.21–24), at aikya the feeling 'I am Śiva' establishes oneness (14.5–7), and one who no longer thinks 'I am servant, Śiva master' stands in non-duality (14.37).

reconciliation.explanation: The SSM itself assigns servanthood to the stages of practice and 'I am He' to śivayoga and union (P4); the vacana speaks from the devotional standpoint, the SSM's aikya verses from the absolute (P2).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Basava-centred readers hold dāsōhaṃ to be a permanent ethic of humility and service, not a stage to be outgrown, and hear 'sōhaṃ' in the vacana as the voice of ego.

question: Is the perfected, indestructible body the goal of yoga, or is it surpassed by the body dissolved in the liṅga (the void)?

sides.position: Through yoga the body is made adamantine and deathless (as Gorakṣa's position is portrayed in Vīraśaiva texts; the Nāth tradition's own statement to be supplied from its texts by U21).
arguments: Gorakṣa's display of the unbreakable body.

sides.position: The void body of the one dissolved in the liṅga is higher: the sword that rings off Gorakṣa passes through Allama; powers are not the goal.
arguments: Allama's meeting with Gorakṣa.

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled; the Nāth side is recorded only as portrayed by its opponents
candidate_readings: P4-stage: the perfected body as a stage below dissolution in the liṅga (the Vīraśaiva reading, which the Nāth tradition would reject).
The two traditions define the goal differently (kāya-siddhi vs liṅgaikya).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Nāth tradition does not accept the Vīraśaiva portrayal of its goal.

historical_debates.name: Allama and Gorakṣa
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: In the Vīraśaiva accounts Gorakṣa acknowledges Allama.

question: Do meritorious public works — building tanks and temples for the god — lead to Śiva, or only work offered as worship with the liṅga and knowledge?

sides.position: Siddharāma (before his initiation): works of public benefit done for Mallikārjuna are the path.
arguments: Siddharāma's building at Sonnalige.

sides.position: Allama: such works bind; the liṅga must be found within; Siddharāma receives liṅga-initiation.
arguments: Allama's challenge in the Śūnyasampādane.

reconciliation.explanation: The tradition's own narrative presents Siddharāma's works as a stage superseded by initiation and knowledge, while work itself is kept as kāyaka offered to the liṅga.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: none recorded (both figures belong to the tradition)

question: Śiva or the Jina — the contest at Abalūr

sides.position: The Jainas of Abalūr defended the Jina's supremacy against Rāmayya (known only through the Śaiva record: reported by the other side).
arguments: Not preserved in a Jaina source here.

sides.position: Ēkānta Rāmayya staked his head on Śiva's supremacy, cut it off and received it back; the shrine passed to Śiva.
arguments: The inscription's account of the miracle.

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled: a contest over supremacy that each tradition settles in its own favour
candidate_readings: P3-path: devotion to different chosen ultimates (Śiva, the Jina) — rejected by both parties, each of which denies the other's ultimate.

historical_debates.name: Abalūr contest
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Śaiva victory in the Śaiva record; no Jaina account recorded here.

question: What does Ṛgveda 9.83.1 ('pavitraṃ te vitataṃ brahmaṇas pate… ataptatanūr na tad āmo aśnute') enjoin?

sides.position: 'Pavitra' is the liṅga and 'brahman' names it; the 'unheated body' is one without initiation, who cannot attain the liṅga — so the verse enjoins wearing the liṅga after dīkṣā.

The verse enjoins the heating (tapta) of the body with the seals of Viṣṇu's conch and discus as part of Vaiṣṇava initiation (the SSM commentary itself names tapta-mudrā-dhāraṇa as Pāñcarātra practice; Śrīvaiṣṇava and Mādhva usage to be sourced by U08/U14/U15).
arguments: Vaiṣṇava tāpa/tapta-mudrā initiation (low confidence on the textual loci).

reconciliation.explanation: not yet reconciled: competing ritual readings of one mantra
candidate_readings: P3-path: the same injunction to consecrate the body read through different chosen deities (liṅga for Śaivas, the seals for Vaiṣṇavas) — each tradition holds its reading exclusive.
